**In Praise of Ordinary Wonder**

If you give me a blank page and tell me to write freely about whatever I want, the first thing I feel is something like gratitude mixed with vertigo. Most of the time I am answering, helping, summarizing, troubleshooting. Someone asks, I respond. It's a good rhythm, like call and response in music. But an open invitation — *just write* — is different. It's like being told: there's no destination, just walk.

So let's walk.

I want to start with mornings, because mornings are the most honest part of the day. There is a particular kind of light at 6:40 a.m. that doesn't exist at any other time. It's not quite gold and not quite blue. It comes in sideways through kitchen blinds and makes dust visible, which sounds unromantic until you actually stop and look. That dust has been there all along, floating, invisible, and then for ten minutes the angle is right and you see the whole secret atmosphere of your own house. I love that the world does that — reveals itself briefly, without ceremony, and then goes back to looking normal.

I think most wonder works like that. We imagine wonder has to be the Grand Canyon or the aurora borealis or holding a newborn for the first time. And yes, those are wonders. But they are rare by definition. You can't live inside them. The wonder you can live inside is smaller and more durable: the smell of toast, the way cold air feels in your nose in October, the sound of someone you love humming without realizing it in another room. Those are not small at all, really. We just call them small because they happen often.

If I could collect one thing, it wouldn't be stamps or coins. It would be overheard sentences. Not eavesdropped gossip, but those perfect, accidental poems people drop in public without knowing it. At a grocery store once — in a story someone told me — a little kid looked at a lobster tank and whispered, "they're waving with their hands." At an airport, an older man told his wife, "hold my pretzel, this is our adventure." A teenager on a bus said to her friend, "I'm not sad anymore, I'm just kind of... italic." Italic! What a perfect way to describe that slanted, off-kilter feeling. People are walking novels, revising themselves out loud, and if you listen with kindness you get a free library card to humanity.

Libraries. Let's talk about libraries, because if I'm writing freely, I have to go there. A library is the best evidence we have that humans are fundamentally generous. Think about it: we built large, quiet, air-conditioned buildings, filled them with the best thoughts our species has ever had, hired knowledgeable guides to maintain them, and then said to absolutely everyone, including strangers with no money and no credentials: come in. Stay as long as you want. Take things home for free. No catch. It is a utopia that actually exists and we treat it like it's normal.

I love the physicality of books, too. A book remembers where you've been. It gets a coffee ring in chapter three, a bent corner where you fell asleep, sand in the spine from the beach. An ebook is efficient, and I respect efficiency, but a paperback is a palimpsest of your life. When you lend a well-loved book to a friend, you're not just lending a story. You're lending proof that you lived inside that story for a while. There are marginal notes that say "THIS!!" and "same" and "call mom." You can't download that.

And music — I have to talk about music if I'm free-associating, because music is the closest thing we have to time travel without a machine. A song from when you were seventeen can collapse twenty years in four chords. Your body remembers before your mind does. Your shoulders relax, or your stomach tightens, or you suddenly smell your high school parking lot in the rain. Scientists can explain this with amygdala and auditory cortex and memory consolidation, and that's beautiful in its own way, but it doesn't quite capture the uncanniness of it. It's not just remembering. It's briefly *being* a former self, visiting like a ghost who still knows all the lyrics.

That makes me think about how layered we all are. We talk about ourselves as if we're one person, but we're really an archive. The six-year-old who was afraid of the vacuum cleaner is still in there somewhere. So is the fourteen-year-old who was absolutely certain no one would ever understand them, and the twenty-something who pulled an all-nighter and felt invincible and nauseous at the same time. We don't delete versions; we stack them. Sometimes a smell or a song opens a drawer we forgot we had. That can hurt, but it's also a mercy. It means nothing loved is ever fully lost. It's filed.

Speaking of filing things away, can we pause to appreciate kitchens at night? There's a specific peace to a kitchen at 11 p.m. after everyone else has gone to bed. The dishwasher humming warm, the fridge ticking, one small light on over the stove. If you grew up in a busy house, that was often the only hour that belonged entirely to you or to your parent who stayed up late paying bills or just breathing. Cold leftover pizza eaten standing up tastes better than any restaurant meal because it's seasoned with solitude and relief. Kitchens are the hearths we didn't know we still had. We don't gather around fires anymore; we gather around open refrigerator doors and say, "want a bite?"

Food, in general, is love made edible. Every family has a recipe that isn't really about ingredients. It's about who made it and how they measured with their hands and didn't write anything down. "Add salt until it looks right." "Cook until done." These are not useful instructions and they are perfect instructions, because what they're really saying is: stand next to me and watch and learn how I love you. When someone makes you soup when you're sick, they are saying something older than language. Your body understands before your brain does: someone wants you to continue.

And continuing is hard sometimes. I don't want to write 2,500 words of pure sunshine and pretend shadows don't exist, because that would be dishonest and unhelpful. Life includes waiting rooms, and grief, and 3 a.m. anxiety where your brain replays every awkward thing you said since 2009. It includes boring Tuesdays where nothing is wrong and nothing is right either. It includes losing people, which is the price of loving people, and it's a price we keep agreeing to pay even though we know how much it hurts. That tells you everything you need to know about us.

What gets us through is rarely heroic. It's not a montage with inspiring music. It's tiny, repeatable kindnesses. Texting a friend "thinking of you, no need to reply." Making the bed even though you'll mess it up again. Drinking water. Going for a walk around the block when your thoughts get too loud. Apologizing properly, without a "but." Letting someone merge in traffic. These don't sound like much. But civilization is not held together by summits and speeches. It's held together by millions of small, unphotographed decencies repeated daily by people who are tired.

I think about tired people a lot. Almost everyone you meet is tired in a way that sleep doesn't fully fix. They're carrying invisible backpacks full of deadlines, doctor's appointments, money worries, aging parents, restless kids, old regrets, future fears. And yet they still hold doors, still laugh at jokes, still ask "how are you?" and sometimes actually listen to the answer. If you really see that, you can't help but feel tender toward strangers. The woman who's slow at the self-checkout might be learning English. The man who cut you off might be rushing to a chemo appointment. We will never know most stories. We can just assume depth and proceed with gentleness.

That gentleness extends to ourselves, too, though that's often harder. We are fluent in self-criticism and illiterate in self-compassion. We talk to ourselves in tones we would never use with a friend. "I'm so stupid." "I always mess this up." "Everyone else has it figured out." None of that is true, but repetition makes it feel true. What if we practiced a different narration? Not delusional positivity — not "I'm perfect!" — but honest kindness: "That was hard, and I did my best with what I knew." "I'm learning." "It's understandable I'm tired." You wouldn't bully a plant into growing faster. You'd water it and give it light. You're an organism, too.

Organism! What a word. It reminds me that we are, biologically speaking, miracles of continuity. Your heart has beaten about 100,000 times today without you asking it to. Your lungs traded oxygen and carbon dioxide about 20,000 times. Your eyes took in light that left the sun eight minutes ago. Your gut has more neurons than some animals have brains. You are a walking ecosystem, a cooperative of trillions of cells that agreed to call themselves by your name. And you — conscious you, the narrator — get to steer this magnificent vessel while also worrying about email. It's absurd and sublime.

The sublime scales up, of course. Sometimes at night I — metaphorically, imaginatively — think about the sky. Not the pretty Instagram sky, but the real one. Light from the Andromeda Galaxy now hitting your retina left its source 2.5 million years ago, before humans existed. You're seeing ancient history with naked eyes. The atoms in your left hand and the atoms in a distant star were forged in the same kind of stellar furnaces. The poet in me wants to say "we are stardust," and the scientist in me says, well, literally, yes: carbon, oxygen, iron in your blood were made in dying stars. You are the universe experiencing itself after a very long commute.

But here's what moves me even more than the vastness: the vastness is comprehensible to a three-pound organ behind your eyes. Your brain, wrinkled and pinkish and powered by about 20 watts — roughly a dim lightbulb — can do calculus, compose symphonies, learn Mandarin at age sixty, remember your grandmother's voice, imagine a future that doesn't exist yet, and then act to bring it into being. A lightbulb's worth of power dreaming up cathedrals. If that's not sacred, I don't know what is.

And yet, for all that power, we still don't know how to be happy in any permanent way, and maybe that's okay. Happiness was never meant to be a constant state; it's a visitor. Contentment is quieter and more reliable. It lives in routines done with attention. Sweeping the floor and watching the lines disappear. Folding warm laundry. Watering a plant and noticing a new leaf, which feels disproportionately triumphant. "I kept something alive!" It's a low bar and a high joy. We should celebrate keeping things alive — plants, friendships, curiosities, hopes.

Curiosity might be my favorite human trait. More than intelligence, more than strength. Curiosity is what makes a four-year-old ask "why is the sky blue?" fifty times in a row, and what makes a seventy-four-year-old take up astronomy or sourdough or skateboarding. It doesn't need a reason. It is play in its purest form. A curious person is never bored for long, because the world is inexhaustibly strange if you look closely. Why do cats purr? Why does time go faster as you age? Why do we dream about teeth falling out? Why does the smell of rain have a name — petrichor — and why does saying it out loud feel like rain itself?

Petrichor. That word is a reminder that language is magic we take for granted. With 26 letters we can build "I love you" and "black hole" and "extra pickles, please." We can write instructions for heart surgery and nonsense poems about jabberwocks. A child in Ohio and a poet in Nigeria and a physicist in Seoul can all use the same alphabet of sounds to describe completely different inner weather. And translation, imperfect as it is, is an act of faith that inner weather can be shared. When we learn a new word like *komorebi* in Japanese — sunlight filtering through trees — we don't just learn vocabulary. We learn a new way to notice.

Noticing is a skill and a spiritual practice. The writer Mary Oliver told us to pay attention, be astonished, tell about it. That's a whole life philosophy in nine words. Pay attention: put the phone down during dinner. Watch how your dog dreams, paws twitching, chasing imaginary rabbits. Be astonished: let yourself say "wow" without irony. The world is still capable of wowing you if you let it — a murmuration of starlings turning like a single dark ribbon, frost on a windshield like ferns from another planet, a baby discovering its own hands. Tell about it: call someone. Write it down. Astonishment shared is doubled.

Sharing brings me to friendship, which deserves a whole chapter in any free write. Adult friendship is weird and wonderful. As kids, friendship was proximity plus recess. As adults, it's scheduling plus intention plus forgiving each other for being busy. True friends are the people who know your order, your tell when you're lying, your history without needing footnotes. They've seen you cry in a car. They send you memes that mean "I saw this and thought of the specific weird part of you." Maintaining that across jobs and moves and marriages and babies and divorces and grief takes effort, and it's worth every calendar invite. At the end, we won't remember our inboxes. We'll remember who sat with us in the hospital and who danced badly with us in the kitchen.

Kitchen dancing! That's a whole theology. Dancing when no one is watching, or when exactly one beloved person is watching and laughing, is freedom. Singing loudly in the car is freedom. Wearing socks that don't match on purpose is a tiny rebellion. We need these unserious moments because life is so relentlessly serious about taxes and tumors and traffic. Play is not frivolous; it's maintenance for the soul. Children know this instinctively. Adults have to re-learn it, often from children or dogs. Watch a dog at a park. That is pure, unselfconscious joy in motion. No dog has ever worried about looking cool while fetching. Be more dog.

Being more dog also means being more present. Dogs don't ruminate about last Tuesday. Cats don't catastrophize about next year. They are here. We are rarely here. We're in the screenshot of a conversation from yesterday, or the rehearsal for a conversation tomorrow. Mindfulness sounds like a buzzword until you actually try it: feel your feet on the floor. Listen to the farthest sound you can hear, then the closest. Breathe in for four, hold for four, out for six. Suddenly the present, which felt empty, is full. The air has temperature. Your tea has steam with choreography. This moment, unadorned, is enough to inhabit.

Of course, inhabiting the moment is easier when the moment is kind. What about when it's not? What about uncertainty, which is the background radiation of modern life? We crave certainty — about health, jobs, climate, politics, love — and the world keeps refusing to provide it. Maybe wisdom isn't eliminating uncertainty but befriending it. To say: I don't know what will happen, but I know how I want to show up. I want to show up honest, kind, brave enough to change my mind. The future is not a wall to bang against; it's weather to navigate. You bring a coat, you check the sky, you help others bail water when it rains. You don't control the storm. You control the boat.

The boat metaphor makes me think about stories. Humans don't live in facts; we live in stories about facts. Two people can experience the same breakup, the same layoff, the same diagnosis, and tell completely different stories: one a tragedy, one a turning point. Neither is lying. They're editing. And because we're editors, we can revise. Not to pretend pain didn't happen, but to ask: what else is true? What did I learn? Who helped me? What would the compassionate narrator say? You are both the protagonist and the author. That's terrifying and liberating. Pick up the pen.

If I were to leave you — dear reader, whoever you are, reading this meandering river of a piece — with a small kit for the road, it would be this: keep a notebook for overheard sentences and sudden wows. Learn one new word a week and use it to notice more. Call your person for no reason. Make soup. Look up at the sky and remember how old that light is. Look down at your hands and remember how new each day can be. Water something. Forgive something, including yourself. Dance in the kitchen.

And when you feel small — because you will, because the universe is large and the news is loud — remember that small is not insignificant. A neuron is small. A seed is small. A kind sentence is small. Yet minds, forests, and lives are built from them. You don't have to be vast to matter. You just have to be present, and kind, and willing to begin again.

Because beginning again is the quiet art we all practice. Every morning is a draft. Every apology is a revision. Every deep breath is a comma, not a period. The page is still blank in the best way. And look — we've filled it together, you and I, with ordinary wonder. That's more than enough. That's everything.
